newsitem.title: KENYA: Coffee prices weak in Uganda, rise in Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices weak in Uganda, rise in Kenya.

text.p: Coffee prices remain largely weak in Uganda, in line with global markets but in contrast with the buoyant trend at Kenya's last export auction of the year.

Traders told Reuters in Nairobi on Monday that November had been a bad month for Uganda's coffee -- with very modest activity blamed on weak international prices. They said the price fall would persist through December.
"During the month of November, the volumes of coffee traded in London and New York were thin, contributing to low activity on the local scene," a senior coffee trader said.
In the last week of November, robusta prices fell to 900-1,000 Ugandan shillings per kg, from 1,100-1,200 earlier.
Prices for the lower Kiboko grades continued to range between 400 and 500, while arabicas slid to 1,100-1,200 from 1,200-1,300 in the first three weeks of November.
"Prices are expected to continue on the downward path because of new coffee supplies from the origins, especially Asia and Africa," another senior trader told Reuters from Kampala.
Kenya's last auction of the year was on December 10.
Senior traders said buyers sustained losses in covering their requirements because higher prices had not been expected.
"The next auction is January 7 and we are told only 18,000 (60-kg) bags will be on offer," a senior trader said.
"That again is lower than expected. What these people (Coffee Board of Kenya) are trying to do is paint a bad picture for prices to keep going up," the trader added.
Another trader said that by January 7 the market position would be very different because millers would be working during the holiday period.
"In the auction that follows, on January 14, perhaps there will be as much as 30,000 bags. The coffee they will try to auction on January 7 is what they have collected now," he said.
At the December 10 auction, premium grade AAs ran to about $63 over March 1997 while ABs ran at around $58-59 over March. Grade Cs were about $52 over March, trade figures showed.
Auctions were postponed on December 3 because of scarce supply.
"Prices are fairly strong and New York is a bit negative -- going down and up a little again. Whoever purchased last week found a very nice hedging deal," a coffee dealer said.

One trader spoke of market talk of declining production in Kenya because of Coffee Berry Disease (CBD) in the key growing central region. Authorities have so far said nothing of the extent of crop losses to the disease.
"This is just talk. People like to portray an image of short positions but in real terms you find enough coffee around," the trader added.
